archetype.name: Retooling (special teams over substance)
archetype.definition: A team that still has a top-line star and an effective power play and penalty kill, but has been outplayed at five-on-five for two straight seasons and is fighting from the bottom of its division.

report.headline: Special teams keep it afloat, but five-on-five has sunk Toronto for two years.
report.take:
Toronto sits 8-12-2, last in the Atlantic and 25th of 32 on the site. This is not a sudden collapse from a good team. Last season was 32-36-14 with a 45.6% expected-goals share and the league's 31st-ranked defense. This year's 5-on-5 numbers are nearly identical: a 46.1% xGF % (27th) and 48% of shot attempts. The decline from the 108-point team of 2024-25 has simply carried over.

The record holds up because of two things. The first is Auston Matthews, 3rd of 240 centers on the site, with 29 points and a 54.4% xGF share on a team that otherwise loses its minutes. The second is special teams. The power play converts 26.7% (6th) and the penalty kill 85.7% (7th), well clear of the league averages of 22.2% and 77.4%. Below that, depth centers and wingers are drowning: Teddy Blueger and Brandon Duhaime sit near 40% xGF. The blue line grades D-. Jake McCabe ranks 231st of 259 defensemen while playing 20 minutes a night, and Chris Tanev's share is 38.6%.

The numbers hide something in both directions. The record is worse than the goals: a -7 differential should have produced more than 18 points, and the Pts vs Goal Diff of -4.3 is 31st in the league. A 5-on-5 PDO of 98.3 also says even-strength bounces have gone against them. But the October that hid the problem was its own mirage. That month they scored 4 goals a game and went 7-7. In November they have scored 1.5 a game and lost all six, with two shutouts in the last five. The all-situations shooting % of .113 is dead average, so neither month is the real offense. Somewhere around three goals a night is.

Where this goes depends on whether the close-game luck evens out before the special teams cool. The PK at 85.7% is well above last year's 81.2%. The power play is running hotter than any season since 2021-22. Both are likelier to drift down than up, and when they do, a team that gives up 28.8 shots a game (26th) has little to fall back on.

strengths.title: Matthews is carrying the team
strengths.body: Matthews has 29 points, 10 on the power play, and a 54.4% expected-goals share. He is the only regular forward clearly above water. His underlying numbers back the production, so it should last. The issue is that the team's 5-on-5 game around him does not.

strengths.title: Elite power play and kill
strengths.body: Both units rank in the league's top seven. The kill sits well above the league average, which is how a team this bad at even strength still has a goal differential ranked 21st. History says the power play can live near this level. The penalty kill is more likely to come back toward last year's 81.2%.

strengths.title: Record lags the goal differential
strengths.body: A Pts vs Goal Diff of -4.3 ranks 31st: Toronto has dropped close games it would usually split. A 5-on-5 PDO of 98.3 points the same way. Expect some points to come back, though not enough to change what kind of team this is.

concerns.title: Losing five-on-five, again
concerns.body: Toronto is 27th in xGF % and 26th in shots allowed. The 45.6% share last season shows this is a second year of the same play, not a slump. Nylander scores, but his 41.2% share and -8 say his line gives it back. Until the even-strength game changes, the team's ceiling is the bubble.

concerns.title: A D- blue line
concerns.body: Four of six regular defensemen post sub-.48 expected-goals shares. McCabe is 231st of 259 on the tab while logging 20 minutes a night. Raddysh plays 24 minutes and sits -12. This group explains the shot volume against, and nothing in the sheet suggests help is coming.

concerns.title: Offense has vanished in November
concerns.body: After scoring 4 a game in October, Toronto has scored 1.5 a game in November. It has just seven goals over the last five games and has been shut out twice. Shooting luck is part of it, and the season shooting % is league-average. But a team without 5-on-5 control cannot afford its power play going quiet.

trend.note: A .500 October, propped up by four goals a game, has given way to an 0-6 November and a six-game losing streak, the longest of the season. Toronto is 2-8 over its last ten.

weekAhead.headline: Three of the league's weakest teams, then the hot-goalie Islanders
weekAhead.body:
This is the softest stretch Toronto will get. Chicago (31st on the site), Los Angeles (30th) and Columbus (27th) come first, and all three have worse goal differentials than the Leafs. Chicago is the worst team in the league by Goal Diff / GP, with F grades at forward and on defense. It also leaks points to wingers more than almost anyone, which suits Nylander, Cowan and the power play. Columbus has the league's lowest shooting % and the 30th-ranked offense, a chance for Bobrovsky to steady himself.

Los Angeles is the trap. The Kings actually win the 5-on-5 battle (50.6% xGF, better than Toronto). Their record is a goaltending story: an F grade and -8.9 GSAx. The Leafs should win the special-teams battle against a 67.2% penalty kill, but they may not control play. The week closes on the road against the Islanders. New York holds forwards well under their averages and gets elite goaltending. Taking anything less than five or six of the first six points would be a bad sign.

keyMatchups.title: Leafs power play vs Kings kill
keyMatchups.body: Toronto's 26.7% power play meets a penalty kill ranked 29th at 67.2%. With the even-strength game tilted toward LA, the power play is where Toronto should decide this one. If the Leafs can't cash in here, the November scoring drought is more than variance.

keyMatchups.title: Wingers against Chicago's leaky defense
keyMatchups.body: Chicago allows wingers nearly a point a game more than their averages imply, 31st in the league. It also sports a .873 save %. Nylander's 11 goals and Cowan's seven make this the likeliest spot for the offense to break out.

keyMatchups.title: Islanders goaltending closes the week
keyMatchups.body: New York's goalies are 3rd in GSAx at +11.9 with a .911 save %. Their penalty kill ranks 4th, which blunts Toronto's best weapon. The Islanders' 102.3 PDO hints they are riding it, but a cold Leafs offense is not the team likely to end that.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal. Stolarz (.906, +0.9 GSAx) has outplayed Bobrovsky (.881, -2.2), and three soft opponents are the time to settle it.

restOfSeason.body:
The current pace, 30 wins and 67 points, overstates the gloom slightly. Toronto has given away points in close games, its 5-on-5 PDO is below average, and shooting and save percentages across all situations are dead league-average. Some of that turns back their way. What does not turn is a 46% expected-goals share and a D- defense, the same profile as last season's 78-point team. Meanwhile the penalty kill and the power play are more likely to slip than climb. Expect something like a .450-.480 points percentage from here: better than November, nowhere near the five teams already clear of them in the division.

That lands Toronto around 72 to 76 points, with a range of roughly 68 to 80. Matthews and the power play give it nights it can win. A blue line that bleeds shots and a starter at .881 make a sustained run unlikely. The Stolarz-Bobrovsky split is the one lever that could move the number meaningfully.
swingFactors: Stolarz taking the bulk of the starts
Whether the penalty kill holds near 85%
Close-game luck flipping back toward even

confidence.note: Only 22 games, but the 5-on-5 profile matches last season's closely.
